title: Sweaty with every feed
objective: Recognize heart failure in the newborn -- tachypnea, feeding difficulty, sweating with feeds, hepatomegaly -- and treat bradycardia and apnea as signs of collapse
secondaryObjectives: Recognize and manage heart failure (high output, congestive, secondary)

brief.situation: 11:00 in the NICU step-down room. You are the nurse for Baby Dubois, a girl born at 38 weeks, now 18 days old, with a large ventricular septal defect awaiting a cardiology review next week. She is bottle-fed every 3 hours.
handover: Her mother says she 'sweats buckets' when she feeds and stops after a few minutes, breathing fast.
Today's weight is the same as four days ago. She had two wet diapers overnight.

The neonatal nurse practitioner covers the room; pediatric cardiology is in house. Unit policy: the nurse may stop an oral feed and give the remainder by the existing gavage tube, raise the head of the bed, and calls the provider at once for apnea, bradycardia or rising work of breathing.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What is going on with Baby Dubois, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: A large VSD at about 2-3 weeks causes heart failure as pulmonary resistance falls: tachypnea, sweating and tiring with feeds, hepatomegaly, a gallop and crackles, and poor weight gain.
parts.modelAnswer: With a big VSD at almost three weeks, she's going into heart failure: fast breathing, sweating and tiring with feeds, a liver that's grown, a gallop and crackles, and she's stopped gaining.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Raises the head, time-limits oral feeds with gavage for the rest, avoids high oxygen, watches for apnea and bradycardia, and calls the provider and cardiology now.
parts.modelAnswer: Head up, short bottle feeds with the rest by gavage, no blasting her with oxygen, watch for apnea or bradycardia, and call the nurse practitioner and cardiology now.

collapse.headline: Apnea and bradycardia
collapse.body: Tachypnea, sweating with feeds, a growing liver and no weight gain are heart failure. Cut the work of feeding and escalate; apnea and bradycardia mean collapse.

safe.headline: Failure recognized and escalated
safe.body: You found the liver, linked the signs to heart failure, cut the energy cost of feeding, avoided hyperoxygenation and called within minutes. That is the expert path.

safeGaps.headline: Escalated, with gaps
safeGaps.body: Check how soon you called, whether she was pushed through a long feed, and whether oxygen was turned up to 100%.

time_up.headline: Unescalated at 12:00
time_up.body: Heart failure signs in an infant with a VSD go to the provider and cardiology now.

scoring.modelReasoning: Infant heart failure shows as poor feeding, sweating with feeds, tachypnea, hepatomegaly, a gallop and tachycardia, with poor weight gain; a large VSD typically declares itself in the first weeks. Reduce the energy cost of feeding (head up, time-limited oral feeds with the rest by gavage), avoid hyperoxygenation in congenital heart disease, and call the provider and cardiology now. Bradycardia, apnea or lethargy are signs of collapse.
